questions.prompt: A user updates their profile, reloads immediately, and sees the old value. Reads go to a replica running 4 seconds behind the primary. Which fix addresses this without adding replication capacity?
options: Route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after their write
Switch the replicas to synchronous replication
Put a cache in front of the replicas
questions.explanation:
Read-your-writes is a routing problem, not a capacity one. Pin the writer's reads to the primary for slightly longer than replication lag and they always observe their own write.

Synchronous replication does fix it, but pays write latency on every write to solve a read-path issue affecting a fraction of requests — that trade is the whole question. More replicas and a cache add capacity or hit rate; neither guarantees a user sees their own write, and a cache can serve data staler still.

questions.prompt: A table has a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at). Which queries can use it efficiently?
options: WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?
questions.explanation:
A composite index is usable left-to-right. Anything that constrains tenant_id first can seek into it; the second column then narrows or orders within that prefix.

Filtering on created_at alone skips the leading column, so the engine has no starting point to seek to and falls back to a scan. This is the most common composite-index mistake: assuming the index helps any query mentioning either column.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a cache-aside read that misses.
items: Application writes the value into the cache
Application returns the value to the caller
questions.explanation:
Cache-aside puts the application in charge: it asks the cache first, and only on a miss does it go to the database and populate the cache itself.

The ordering matters because the cache is never in the write path to the database. That is what makes the pattern easy to reason about — and also why it can serve stale data until the entry expires.
